Chapter 9: Freedom from Opinion — Letting Go of Others’ Judgments
Imagine sitting with a trusted mentor, just talking about the things that weigh you down. At one point, the younger friend opens up about something we all know too well—the fear of what other people think. He admits his mood swings up and down with every bit of praise or criticism, and how exhausting it is to try to keep everyone happy.
The mentor listens, nodding—because he’s been there, too. He shares a story about a colleague who was always chasing approval. This person changed his opinions just to fit in, never daring to stand out. But after a while, all that constant shifting left him drained, confused, and unsure of who he really was.
Then, he contrasts this with someone else—a person who, even though he was sometimes misunderstood, held onto his own values. And you know what? That gave him a quiet sort of confidence.
The mentor points out something powerful: real freedom isn’t about getting everyone to like you. It’s about letting go of that need in the first place. Most people are so busy worrying about how they come across that they lose track of what they actually believe in. But when you start trusting your own judgment, suddenly, other people’s opinions just don’t have the same hold over you.
He encourages his friend—and really, all of us—to remember that everyone sees the world through their own unique lens. Their views are shaped by their own fears, hopes, and experiences. What makes one person happy might upset someone else. So, trying to please everybody? That’s just setting yourself up for frustration.
The mentor offers a simple, practical tip: next time you’re criticized, pause. Don’t react right away. Ask yourself, “Is there any truth in this?” If there is, use it as a chance to grow. If not, just let it go. Yeah, it’s not always easy, but with practice, that sting of judgment really does start to fade.
He also warns about falling into the trap of always seeking validation. He remembers a performer who lived for applause, but felt completely empty once the audience was gone. True satisfaction, he says, comes from living by your own values—not by chasing approval from the crowd.
And finally, the mentor leaves his friend with a gentle reminder: the only opinion that truly matters is your own. When you let go of other people’s judgments, you open the door to living authentically—and finding a freedom that no one else can give or take away.
